articles.title: In 1939, a California family bought a Joseph Kleitsch painting from his widow for $100; 75 years later, their daughter brought it to Antiques Roadshow and heard a $500,000 valuation
articles.summary: A painting bought for just $100 in 1939 turned into one of the more remarkable discoveries featured on PBS’ Antiques Roadshow.
articles.body: A painting bought for just $100 in 1939 turned into one of the more remarkable discoveries featured on PBS’ Antiques Roadshow. The work, by Hungarian-born California Impressionist Joseph Kleitsch, was brought to the programme decades later by the daughter of the couple who originally purchased it. In 2014, New York-based art expert Debra Force gave the painting a retail valuation of $500,000. The PBS Antiques Roadshow archive confirms the original purchase, the provenance and the 2014 valuation, while later reporting by Outdoor Painter and Grunge provides additional details about the artwork’s history and what happened to it afterwards.A $100 painting with an extraordinary historyThe painting, dating to around 1925, depicts a scene from Laguna Beach, California, during a period when Kleitsch was documenting the rapidly developing coastal community. It is now identified as The Drugstore, a 40-by-40-inch oil on canvas showing Rankin’s drugstore and other buildings against a landscape of trees.Its journey into the family’s hands was unusually direct. The woman who appeared on Antiques Roadshow explained that her parents knew Kleitsch and his widow. They purchased the painting from the artist’s widow in 1939, eight years after Kleitsch’s death.That provenance became an important part of the painting’s appeal. Instead of an artwork with an uncertain ownership trail, the family could trace it directly back to Kleitsch’s widow. Later accounts also reported that the family retained the original bill of sale, further strengthening its history.Why Joseph Kleitsch’s work matteredKleitsch was born in Hungary and studied art in Budapest, Paris and Munich before coming to the United States. He initially worked largely as a portrait painter, but his artistic direction changed after he moved to Southern California around 1920.Laguna Beach became particularly important to him. His paintings captured the town, its buildings, people and surrounding landscape during a period when it was still a relatively small coastal community. According to the Antiques Roadshow account, Kleitsch was also known for his use of colour and expressive brushwork.His career was relatively short. Kleitsch died suddenly in 1931 at the age of 49, which has contributed to the rarity of his California paintings. Art historians have subsequently regarded him as an important figure in California Impressionism.The subject of this particular work makes it especially interesting. The Drugstore records a piece of early Laguna Beach history, depicting Rankin Drugstore at a time when the area looked dramatically different from the California coastal destination known today. Outdoor Painter reported that the building stood near what was then the unpaved Pacific Coast Highway.The surprising Antiques Roadshow valuationWhen the painting appeared on Antiques Roadshow in New York in 2014, Force examined both the artwork and its provenance. The programme recorded a retail valuation of $500,000. That figure was not an auction result or a confirmed sale price. It represented the expert’s estimate of what the painting could command in a gallery, particularly in California, where Kleitsch’s work had a strong collecting base.The distinction matters because Antiques Roadshow valuations are estimates rather than guaranteed selling prices. The programme itself notes that values can change depending on factors such as condition, market demand and where an object is sold. Still, the difference between the family’s original $100 purchase and the 2014 estimate was striking. The painting had remained with the family for roughly 75 years before its appearance on television.What happened to the painting afterwardsThe story did not end with the television appraisal. Following the episode, interest in the painting increased, and the work eventually changed hands. According to later reporting, John and Patricia Dilks acquired The Drugstore in 2016. The exact sale price was not publicly disclosed, although reports indicate that it sold for more than the $500,000 television valuation.The painting subsequently entered the public eye again through museum exhibitions. It was displayed at the Irvine Museum in 2016 as part of an exhibition of California art and was later included in a 2023 Laguna Art Museum exhibition devoted to Kleitsch’s work.What began as a $100 family purchase in 1939 had therefore become something considerably more significant: not just a valuable painting, but a rare visual record of early Laguna Beach and an important surviving work by an artist whose career ended far too soon.You use AI every day. articles.title: “The Bihari in me said, ‘I’ll come back when your President invites me’”: When Sharad Sagar left US to work in India, people laughed, but he manifested the future
articles.summary: When Sharad Vivek Sagar was finishing his education in the US and preparing to return to Bihar, some of his American friends could not understand his
articles.body: When Sharad Vivek Sagar was finishing his education in the US and preparing to return to Bihar, some of his American friends could not understand his decision. Why leave behind the possibility of a well-paid job, a Manhattan high-rise office and the lifestyle that came with it?A decade later, Sagar has recalled what he told them at the time - a line that sounded more like a joke than a promise.“The Bihari I was, I would tell them, I would come back when your president invites me,” Sagar says in a video shared on Instagram, recalling the years when he was studying in the US.That invitation eventually came. On September 16, 2016, Sagar received an invitation from the White House to attend a special gathering hosted by then US President Barack Obama. Sagar revisited the moment through an instagram post and recalled it as one of the most unexpected turns in his journey.“In September, around that time, I was in the state of West Bengal,” he recalled in the video. “That morning at 5 a.m., I received an invite from the White House saying that the president would like to invite me to a special gathering of leaders.”The invitation was for South by South Lawn: A White House Festival of Ideas, Art and Action, an event held at the White House on October 3, 2016. The gathering brought together creators, innovators and organisers working on ideas aimed at improving people's lives. Contemporary reports identified Sagar as the only Indian invited to the event.For Sagar, however, the significance of the invitation went beyond the White House address. “I was the only Indian invited, and it was just such a remarkable honor,” he says in the video.From Bihar to the White HouseBy the time Obama invited him, Sagar was already known for his work in education and youth development. He had founded Dexterity Global in 2008, at the age of 16, with a focus on creating opportunities for students and helping young people develop skills and access higher-education opportunities.In 2016, he had also graduated from Tufts University in Massachusetts, where he studied international relations and diplomacy. The Telegraph reported at the time that Dexterity Global worked to create opportunities for students through programmes focused on entrepreneurship, leadership, skills and access to universities.But Sagar's latest recollection begins much earlier - with the reaction of friends who thought he was giving up a more conventional version of success. “When I was graduating and coming back, returning to Bihar, my American friends would tell me that you are such an idiot,” he says.He remembers the argument they made: after receiving a strong education in the US, why return without first earning money and building a conventional career? “You just received such a great education and you're going back without earning money and like working out of a Manhattan high-rise building, getting those fat paychecks, driving those German cars,” Sagar recalls them telling him.“And when would you come back to the U.S.?” His answer, he says, was characteristically direct. “And the Bihari I was, I would tell them, I would come back when your president invites me.”The 5am White House emailThe remark might have remained a memorable exchange between friends had the invitation never arrived. Instead, years later, Sagar found himself waking up to a message from the White House.The timing made the moment even more striking. He was in West Bengal when the invitation came.“In September, around that time, I was in the state of West Bengal. That morning at 5 a.m., I received an invite from the White House,” he says.The invitation was not for a conventional political meeting. Obama’s South by South Lawn was designed as a gathering around ideas, innovation, art and social change. The White House event was described at the time as bringing together people who were working to improve lives through their work.For the young entrepreneur from Bihar, the invitation also represented an unusual full circle.In an interview published in 2016, Sagar said Obama had influenced him as a leader and described the invitation as a great honour.A decade later, his recollection focuses less on the glamour of the moment and more on the improbability of what had happened: a casual-sounding promise made to friends had, against the odds, come true.Sagar had chosen to return to India after his education rather than follow the conventional path his friends expected of him. His work through Dexterity Global had kept him focused on education and opportunities for young people.And then came the invitation he had once jokingly set as the condition for returning to America.“The Bihari I was, I would tell them, I would come back when your president invites me,” he says.Ten years after that invitation, it is the line that perhaps best captures the story he now looks back on - not simply of reaching the White House, but of a young man from Bihar deciding that returning home was not a step backwards.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday said his government would introduce stringent laws against what he termed “love jihad”
articles.body: NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday said his government would introduce stringent laws against what he termed “love jihad” and “land jihad” within six months and implement a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in the state.Speaking at an event marking the birth centenary of former VHP president Ashok Singhal, Adhikari said West Bengal would follow Uttarakhand and Gujarat in implementing the UCC.“Give us six months, will also bring stringent laws against love and land jihad,” news agency PTI quoted him as saying.The state government has already set up a high-level committee headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai to examine a draft UCC.The proposed legislation seeks to bring uniformity in civil laws relating to marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption across communities.Adhikari said his government would function within the Constitution but would not tolerate attacks on Indian culture, traditions, temples and monasteries.“This government will not allow any anti-national activity here,” he said, urging people to remain united and vigilant against what he called “divisive forces”.“You can rest assured that the government will function in accordance with the Constitution. But it will not allow any attack on Indian culture, Sanatani traditions, temples and monasteries, and our heritage that spiritual icons Vivekananda and Mahaprabhu Sri Chaitanya have propounded.”The BJP had made implementation of the UCC one of its key promises in the 2026 West Bengal assembly elections.Adhikari also announced plans for a religious tourism circuit, saying the project would be completed within two years with Rs 1,000 crore earmarked for it.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: US man convicted of killing motorist to be resentenced after court rejects AI video of victim forgiving him
articles.summary: An Arizona man convicted of fatally shooting a motorist during a road-rage confrontation will be resentenced after an appeals court ruled that an
articles.body: An Arizona man convicted of fatally shooting a motorist during a road-rage confrontation will be resentenced after an appeals court ruled that an AI-generated video of the victim addressing him should not have been shown in court.Gabriel Paul Horcasitas, 55, was convicted of killing 37-year-old Christopher Pelkey during a confrontation at a traffic light in 2021. He was sentenced to about 10 years in prison, but challenged the sentence after the trial judge allowed Pelkey's family to present an AI-generated video of the dead victim during the sentencing hearing. The BBC and Reuters reported that the Arizona Court of Appeals upheld Horcasitas' conviction but ordered a fresh sentencing hearing.The three-judge appeals panel said the AI video went beyond a conventional victim-impact statement because it presented thoughts attributed to Pelkey that he had never actually expressed. The court said the use of the video made the sentencing procedure "fundamentally unfair".What did the AI video show?Pelkey's family created the video using his photographs, videos and voice recordings. It showed an AI-generated version of Pelkey wearing a grey baseball cap and speaking directly to Horcasitas."To Gabriel Horcasitas, the man who shot me, it is a shame we encountered each other that day in those circumstances. In another life, we probably could have been friends," the AI version of Pelkey said."I believe in forgiveness, and a God who forgives. I always have and I still do," it added.Pelkey's sister Stacey Wales had earlier told the BBC that the family created the video to portray her brother and communicate the impact his death had on those around him.Why did court reject AI video?The appeals court said the video was different from an actual recording of Pelkey or a reconstruction of something he had said while alive. Instead, it depicted his imagined thoughts, based on material created by his sister."Rather than document an event or recording a particular moment, the AI video presents a depiction of the victim and his thoughts created from the imaginings of the victim's sister," the court said.The trial judge, Todd Lang, had appeared to respond positively to the video during the sentencing. "I loved that AI, thank you for that," Lang said, adding that he heard forgiveness in the message.The appeals ruling does not overturn Horcasitas' manslaughter conviction. His sentence will now be determined again by a lower court without the disputed AI video.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Russia stood by us when our territorial integrity was under threat': Jaishankar
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday highlighted India's longstanding ties with Russia, saying the country had stood by us when New
articles.body: NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday highlighted India's longstanding ties with Russia, saying the country had stood by us when New Delhi's security and territorial integrity faced threats and much of the world preferred backing a military regime.Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting, Jaishankar said India and Russia had maintained strong relations since the 1950s and that the legacy of those ties continued to shape the relationship.“India and Russia have historically very good relations, particularly since the 1950s. That history is not forgotten,” Jaishankar said.He added that Russia which was Soviet Union before “stood by us in many ways when our security, when our territorial integrity was under threat”.“At a time when much of the world preferred backing a military regime (Pakistan) next to us, Russia was a country with which our relations were very good, and we are shaped in many ways by that legacy,” he said.“Today, the relationship has widened beyond that... It is very much more today an economic relationship as well. So there is a military component, there are nuclear component, there is space issues, but there is a significant amount of trade and investment between the two countries and energy and resources as well... India's experience has been quite positive and consistently positive” he added.Jaishankar also said India had moved beyond simply advocating dialogue and diplomacy to taking a more active role in efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict.He said India had held conversations with both Kyiv and Moscow in recent months and was trying to address some immediate concerns arising from the conflict.“Our position on that conflict has been very clear, which is that we would like to see an end to this conflict. This will require dialogue and diplomacy. There has to be negotiations in this regard,” he said.“We have been advocating it for many years, and in recent months we have got a little bit more involved beyond advocacy. We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard. We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue,” he added.Jaishankar said India's efforts were focused initially on ensuring the safety of shipping in the Black Sea, while also addressing issues related to grain and energy exports.“India is going beyond that to cover some immediate concerns which both of them (Russia and Ukraine) have on grain exports, energy exports, non-attack possibilities. Those are ongoing conversations right now,” he said.His remarks came days after Russian President Vladimir Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi had “good ideas” for finding a mutually acceptable solution to the conflict.Ukraine foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had also said on Friday that Kyiv received separate proposals from India and three other countries on a possible ceasefire. India has for more than four years maintained that the Ukraine conflict should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, PTI reported.PM Modi held wide-ranging talks with Putin in Bishkek on August 31. During the meeting, the Prime Minister stated that “endless war must now give way to end of war”.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Yemen launches major military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory as fighting intensifies
articles.summary: Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced the start of military operations to retake territory held by the Iran-aligned Houthis, as
articles.body: Yemen's internationally recognised government has announced the start of military operations to retake territory held by the Iran-aligned Houthis, as government forces said they were conducting strikes in the capital Sanaa and the Houthi stronghold of Saada.The head of Saudi-backed Yemen's presidential council, Rashad al-Alimi, announced the operation in a televised address on Sunday, saying the objective was to restore state authority across the country.“Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory,” al-Alimi said.A spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces, which are aligned with the internationally recognised government, said forces were targeting what he described as “vital targets” in Sanaa and Saada, without providing further details.Houthi-run Al Masirah TV earlier reported an attack on Sanaa that it said was carried out by Saudi Arabia. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the reported strike.Also Read| OPEC+ keeps November oil output targets steady as Iran war hits supplyThe announcement follows a renewed escalation in Yemen's civil war. Fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and forces aligned with the Saudi-backed government had largely subsided after a 2022 truce, but hostilities have intensified again amid the wider conflict involving Iran and the United States.Following al-Alimi’s announcement, heavy ground fighting broke out in Yemen’s Kahboub Mountains overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, with government forces backed by al-Subaiha tribesmen clashing with Houthi fighters, Al Jazeera reported.The Houthis have also made territorial gains in recent weeks, including along Yemen's Red Sea coast, while fighting has intensified around the government-held city of Taiz.Earlier on Sunday, four security sources told AFP that Houthi forces had cut a key supply route linking Taiz with Aden, the interim capital of Yemen's internationally recognised government.“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area told AFP.Three Yemeni military sources also confirmed Houthi control of the area and the supply route, saying traffic had been halted on the main road between Taiz and Aden while fighting continued.“They've achieved the military objective of isolating Taiz from Aden, even if they haven't fully taken control of it,” Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, told AFP.The Houthis have separately claimed missile and drone attacks on Saudi targets, including Saudi Aramco facilities in Riyadh and the Khurais area, saying they were carried out in response to Saudi-led strikes in Yemen.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar intensified in Delhi on Sunday, with AAP workers, AISA and NSUI
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar intensified in Delhi on Sunday, with AAP workers, AISA and NSUI activists among those detained as demonstrators attempted to march towards Jantar Mantar for the third consecutive day.AAP workers, members of its student wing ASAP, NSUI workers, AISA activists and members of other organisations took part in the demonstrations, prompting heavy deployment of Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel across central Delhi.The protests are part of a wider agitation over alleged irregularities in the Election Commission’s functioning, the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and alleged mass deletion of voters.Here are the top developmentsAISA stages protestAISA members and activists from several organisations marched from the Ashoka Road area towards Jantar Mantar but were stopped by police barricades.The protesters briefly clashed with security personnel as they tried to cross the barricades. AISA national president Neha Bora was among those seen attempting to breach the police cordon. Senior advocates Prashant Bhushan and Kapil Sibal also participated in the protest.The mobilisation began from Andhra Bhawan Circle on Ashoka Road, with protesters raising slogans against Kumar and demanding his resignation.Neha Bora detainedAISA members later alleged that Bora was taken away in a private vehicle and that her whereabouts were initially unknown.The organisation said the detention took place as its activists attempted to return to Jantar Mantar for the third consecutive day despite heavy barricading and security arrangements.Visuals showed Bora attempting to climb over a barricade as police officials tried to stop her.Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke slammed Delhi Police for detaining Bora, saying it has “once again shown cowardice”.In a post on X, Dipke said, “Delhi Police has once again shown its cowardice by detaining Neha and Rosy for simply raising their voices. Rosy yesterday was molested by ACP Vivek Bhagat and instead of acting against the pervert, the cops detained her.“So much for women empowerment Narendra Modi,” he added.AAP workers detained at India GateMore than a dozen AAP workers were detained during the protest at India Gate, including Delhi unit chief Saurabh Bharadwaj and MLA Sanjeev Jha. Visuals from the protest showed AAP workers blocking buses carrying detained protesters as security personnel tried to clear the area. The situation escalated when protesters broke through barricades and moved towards Jantar Mantar, where Delhi Police and the Rapid Action Force were deployed to stop them.Bharadwaj alleged that police manhandled him during the detention and said protesters were being treated harshly.“They are picking me up and throwing me around like I am a football... There is such a large police force here, yet they are not even registering an FIR against their own ACP, nor are they arresting the ACP,” he said.Bharadwaj also shared a photograph on X, saying he had been turned upside down by Delhi Police at India Gate to hide his face from cameras.“These are my shoes in the air,” he said.AAP chief Arvind Kejriwal criticised the police action on X, saying, “This is absolutely shocking. Modi ji has left even Hitler behind.”Female journalists allege sexual harassmentThe protests have also triggered a controversy over allegations of sexual harassment and misconduct by police personnel during Saturday’s demonstrations.Three women identifying themselves as journalists complained that they were manhandled and sexually harassed by police officers while covering the protests near Jantar Mantar on October 3.Delhi Police said the complaints had been received, medical examinations conducted and the matter transferred to the Crime Branch for a “fair and impartial enquiry”.CPM leader Brinda Karat criticised the police over the handling of the complaints and questioned the reported demand for video evidence before registering an FIR.“Now, when sexual harassment is happening with a journalist and Delhi Police is trying to save him and it is being asked to show the video,” Karat said, calling the response “extremely wrong”.Opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, have also criticised the alleged police conduct and demanded accountability.Over 500 detained on FridayMore than 500 protesters, including student activists and political leaders, were detained during demonstrations in central Delhi on Friday. articles.summary: Former Maharashtra chief minister and senior Congress leader Prithviraj Chavan on Sunday rejected Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray’s
articles.body: Former Maharashtra chief minister and senior Congress leader Prithviraj Chavan on Sunday rejected Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray’s call to boycott elections, saying participation in elections was a democratic right.“I do not accept that we should boycott the election. It is our right to a democratic government; that is not a correct strategy,” Chavan said.Chavan made the remarks amid a political confrontation over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Maharashtra and the functioning of the Election Commission. On Sunday, Raj Thackeray and Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray led a joint protest march in Mumbai against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, demanding the cancellation of the SIR exercise and raising questions over the poll panel’s functioning.Recalling the 2024 election, Chavan said he had raised concerns over alleged duplicate voters being added to electoral rolls and voting multiple times.“When my election took place in 2024, I protested, saying in my case duplicate voters were added who voted multiple times,” he said.Chavan further alleged that some minority and poor voters had been denied their voting rights, including people who supported the Congress.“In some places, minority voters were deprived of voting rights; in some places, poor people were deprived of voting rights; those who favoured the Congress party,” he said.“This is not vote chori; it is election chori,” Chavan alleged.His remarks came as the Thackeray cousins jointly led what was described as the ‘Virat Garjana Morcha’ in Mumbai, with Congress and NCP (SP) leaders also participating. Raj Thackeray called for the SIR exercise in Maharashtra to be scrapped and for elections to return to ballot papers.“Our demand is that the entire SIR conducted in Maharashtra should be cancelled,” Raj Thackeray said.“The law says that SIR is conducted if an emergency situation arises,” he said, questioning the circumstances in which the revision was undertaken.Raj Thackeray also alleged that 40 to 60 lakh voters were added during the Maharashtra Assembly elections and claimed that two crore voters were now being removed through SIR.“Forty to sixty lakh voters were added during the Assembly elections, and power was captured through this. And now, through SIR, two crore people are being removed. Who are these two crore voters?” he asked.Uddhav Thackeray separately questioned the appointment process for Election Commissioners and criticised the removal of the Chief Justice of India from the selection committee.“The first question is how was Gyanesh Kumar appointed?” Thackeray asked.The Election Commission has maintained that the electoral-roll revision is intended to update and clean the rolls, with mechanisms available for claims and objections.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: After Donald Trump’s second-term climate cuts scrapped billions in research grants and left thousands of federal workers jobless, Climate Reserve stepped in with new roles for 50 climate experts
articles.summary: The United States’ climate science community faced a dramatic upheaval after President Donald Trump began his second term, with his administration cutting
articles.body: The United States’ climate science community faced a dramatic upheaval after President Donald Trump began his second term, with his administration cutting billions of dollars in research funding and firing thousands of federal employees across agencies including the Environmental Protection Agency and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. For climate scientists and officials who suddenly found themselves without jobs or funding, the changes came as a major shock. But amid the uncertainty, a group of former government officials and climate experts began working on an unusual solution: creating a new network to keep climate research alive outside the federal government.People were “in shock,” said Aparna Shrivastava, a former senior climate official in the Biden administration. As she spoke privately with dozens of climate experts who had lost their jobs or funding, many were still determined to continue studying a rapidly warming planet and finding ways to address its consequences. Yet the sudden cuts had left them with few options.The question they kept returning to was simple: “What could we possibly do to address this?” Shrivastava said.(This story was originally published by Grist.)More than 30 experts come together to find a solutionThe conversations eventually moved beyond private chats. At a workshop convened by the Aspen Global Change Institute in Colorado last July, more than 30 climate experts began discussing ways to support colleagues who had been laid off and prevent important research from disappearing.That effort eventually became the Climate Reserve, an initiative backed by tens of millions of dollars and led by Shrivastava. The organization is now making its work public as it seeks to expand its network and provide new opportunities for climate experts affected by the federal cuts.Climate Reserve operates as a network designed to identify climate research and other critical work that has been left in limbo and find institutions where it can continue without federal support.Sometimes, that means helping a climate researcher move into a position at an environmental nonprofit or university. In other cases, it means finding a new home for projects that were removed from government budgets.Climate Reserve has already funded more than two dozen positionsSo far, Climate Reserve has funded more than two dozen positions for climate experts, known as fellows. They are now working at organizations across the country, including the Environmental Protection Network and the University of Minnesota.The group has also helped revive projects that were affected by federal funding cuts. One example is EJScreen, an online mapping tool that identifies communities across the United States experiencing some of the worst pollution. The now-independent tool is being kept up to date with support from the network.The Climate Reserve’s work extends beyond the US as well. Its projects include mapping sea-level rise on islands in Panama and measuring greenhouse gas emissions across five African countries.However, not all of its work is being made public. Organizers have maintained some secrecy around certain fellows and projects, partly out of concern that people who still rely on federal funding or hope to apply for it in the future could find themselves in the crosshairs of the Trump administration.‘So many people are still out of work’As the initiative has grown, its organizers have become more willing to publicly discuss their efforts in the hope of attracting additional funding.The scale of the job losses remains apparent in unexpected places. Shrivastava recalled that even a Lyft driver who took her to the airport in Washington, D.C., while she was traveling to meet potential funders turned out to be a laid-off climate and energy expert.The Climate Reserve name itself reflects the group's emergency-response philosophy. Brittany Janis, executive director of the nonprofit Open Environmental Data Project and one of the participants in the initiative's early discussions, said the name was meant to evoke both a nature reserve and the Army Reserve.It is “the emergency group that you can call up to bring people together,” Janis said.Her organization has partnered with Climate Reserve to hire a former senior adviser for environmental justice programs in the Biden administration to maintain the independent EJScreen tool.Former federal workers get a ‘parachute’For Climate Reserve, the goal is not simply to provide jobs. Organizers also want to prevent the loss of specialized knowledge built up by scientists and government officials over years of public service.Janis described the positions as a kind of “parachute” that allows former federal workers to land in organizations where their experience can continue to be used.“How can we be really thoughtful about parachuting people to the right places so we aren’t losing all that institutional knowledge and that really critical basis for climate action in the U.S.?” she said.The group is also trying to encourage collaboration rather than competition among climate organizations that are now operating with fewer resources.Ben Poulter, who leads an emissions-monitoring program at climate solutions nonprofit Spark, said the founders recognized early on that the funding cuts could further divide the climate research community.“We realized early on that the changes that were happening could fragment the community even further as resources became scarcer,” Poulter said. “The whole point of Climate Reserve is that we’re all in the same boat and we need to work together.”Climate experts share resources instead of competingSeveral of the group's founders have described this approach as “movement generosity” - a philosophy centered on sharing expertise and resources to advance the broader goals of climate research.Under the model, one expert funded by Climate Reserve could potentially divide their time between two organizations, allowing the groups to coordinate projects and avoid unnecessary duplication.Poulter, who previously coordinated greenhouse gas monitoring efforts between federal agencies, is now working on research into how climate-sensitive ecosystems such as wetlands could release increasing amounts of planet-warming emissions as temperatures rise.One Climate Reserve fellow at Spark will help coordinate measurements across five African countries, while another will work on translating the findings into policy recommendations, Poulter said.Saving the ‘unsexy’ work behind climate scienceSome of the work being supported by Climate Reserve is far removed from the headlines but remains essential to climate research.Sonia Wang, who leads the Center for Climate and Environmental Data at the Data Foundation, said the organization is helping preserve important data-crunching projects that can determine whether scientists and policymakers can trust climate information.For example, two groups using satellites to detect methane emissions could reach different conclusions if they rely on different wind-speed models.Resolving such discrepancies may not attract much attention, but it is critical to producing reliable climate data.“It's not the flashiest thing, but when you look under the hood, this is really what’s necessary,” Wang said.The Data Foundation has taken on four Climate Reserve-funded experts to work on projects aimed at improving the reliability and consistency of climate data.Climate Reserve aims to place 50 experts in new rolesThe initiative is now expanding quickly. By the end of the month, Climate Reserve expects to have placed 50 climate experts in new positions, Shrivastava said. The group also plans to triple its funding by the end of next year.Its organizers say the long-term goal is not to permanently replace federal climate research. Instead, they hope to create a more resilient network that can continue supporting scientists and projects during political shifts.“If federal support for climate research eventually returns,” the network could help make the field more collaborative and resilient in the future, according to the initiative's organizers.“We are not at all looking to replace the government. We’re just stepping up to try and meet some of the needs here,” Shrivastava said.‘The need is only going to get stronger’For climate and health experts who spent years working inside the federal government, the transition has meant finding new ways to continue public service.John Balbus, a Climate Reserve fellow, spent 15 years in the federal government. Most recently, he served as a senior official at the Department of Health and Human Services, where he coordinated efforts addressing the health effects of climate change, including extreme heat and wildfire smoke.He is now continuing that work through the Federation of American Scientists and as an independent consultant.Balbus said climate change may remain politically divisive in the United States, but its consequences affect everyone. The climate and health experts he previously worked with, he said, would “do anything in their human power” to continue a life of public service even without government jobs.And as climate risks continue to grow, the demand for their expertise is unlikely to disappear.“The need is only going to get stronger every year,” Balbus said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mute-deaf boy goes missing from govt shelter home in city, probe ordered
articles.summary: 12-year-old mute-deaf boy missing from Patna’s Apna Ghar shelter home; police filed FIR, reviewing CCTV and security as search continues.
articles.body: Patna: A 12-year-old boy, who is mute and deaf, has gone missing from Apna Ghar, a shelter home run by the social welfare department in Shastri Nagar area of Patna, prompting police to launch a search operation and examine security arrangements at the facility.According to officials, the child was reported missing from the shelter home, located behind Lalit Bhawan near Bailey Road, on the evening of Oct 2. He was last seen on the rooftop of the premises before disappearing.Following a complaint lodged by the shelter home’s superintendent, a team from Shastri Nagar police station reached the facility and began an investigation.Shastri Nagar SHO Prashant Kumar Bhardwaj said an FIR was registered on Sunday and efforts were underway to trace the child. “It is not yet clear how the child escaped, but we are certain he did not leave through the main gate. We are examining CCTV footage of the premises and conducting raids to recover him,” Bhardwaj told TOI.As part of the inquiry, ASI Ajit Kumar reviewed security arrangements at the shelter home. Four home guards are deployed at the facility, but they are not permitted to enter beyond the main gate.According to the roster, ApnaGhar currently houses 71 children, including 42 children with disabilities and 29 others.Police said they are not only searching for the missing child but also examining the circumstances surrounding the incident and the adequacy of supervision and security arrangements at the shelter home. The child had not been traced till Sunday evening.Meanwhile, a home guard posted at the facility, Golu, alleged lapses in the care and supervision of children and claimed they were not being properly looked after. articles.title: Deer alarms ring across Buxa after decades as ‘shy’ tigress finally steps out of her enclosure
articles.summary: Reintroduced tigress from Valmiki exits enclosure in Buxa Tiger Reserve, monitored by GPS collar; spotted deer alarm calls signal predator’s return.
articles.body: Kolkata: In what could be the first such instance in many years, spotted deer alarm calls were sounded in Buxa Tiger Reserve as the reintroduced tigress walked out of her enclosure on Sunday, signalling the return of a predator that the forest’s prey might not have encountered in years.The three-year-old tigress, brought to Buxa from Bihar’s Valmiki, walked out of her 2.2-hectare enclosure around 4.50 pm, two days after the doors were opened.Foresters had decided not to rush the tigress into the wild and instead allowed her to acclimatise to the surroundings. “She walked out casually and sprayed on a tree along the way,” a source said.The tigress is being closely monitored through a GPS-enabled radio collar. Ground teams are tracking her using a very high frequency (VHF) transmitter. It will alert foresters if she approaches or crosses the forest boundary.The enclosure lies in the reserve’s core area, with villages such as 28 Mile and Jayanti located around 8-12km away.Officials believe the tigress’s shy nature could reduce the immediate risk of human-animal conflict. During her capture in Valmiki, it took several days for her to kill the bait calf, approaching it cautiously when she eventually made the kill, said a source. articles.title: America’s Arctic war machine roars to life as commander reveals chilling new reality on Russia’s doorstep
articles.summary: U.S. and Canadian forces deploy HIMARS, F-35s and F-16s across western Alaska as Tundra Merlin tests rapid American Arctic combat readiness.
articles.body: Across one of the coldest, most remote and strategically exposed corners of the United States, American forces are practicing how to fight on land, at sea and in the air — rapidly moving rocket systems into western Alaska, sending F-35s and F-16s toward simulated threats and coordinating U.S. and Canadian warships in the Bering Sea. The operations are part of Tundra Merlin, an enduring U.S. military campaign aimed at proving that even across Alaska’s vast distances and extreme Arctic conditions, American and allied forces can rapidly assemble combat power to defend the northern approaches to the homeland. And behind that show of force is a changing security environment increasingly shaped by Russia and China. TWO ICEBREAKERS HEADED TO ALASKA AS US COMBATS RUSSIAN, CHINESE INFLUENCE IN ARCTIC "I think what’s changed is primarily two things," Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, told Fox News Digital. "One is that the melting sea ice has made the Arctic more accessible. And we’re seeing increased activity both commercially and militarily in the Arctic, particularly during the summer months." "The other factor is that China and Russia and others are continuing to advance their military capabilities and capacity with an interest in showing that they can use them in the Arctic as well," Davis said. The Pentagon has reached a similar conclusion. Its 2024 Arctic Strategy warned that growing Russia-China cooperation could "alter the Arctic’s stability and threat picture," and called for greater U.S. presence, exercises and military preparedness in a region becoming increasingly accessible. Defense officials have said forces operating there must be able not merely to train in extreme conditions, but survive them. RUSSIA PULLED BACK FROM THE ARCTIC, FOR NOW. NATO MUST ACT BEFORE THOSE TROOPS RETURN Few places illustrate the stakes better than Alaska. The state sits at the intersection of the Arctic and Pacific and serves as a critical hub for homeland defense and a platform for projecting U.S. military power toward the Indo-Pacific and beyond. The Russian and American mainlands are only about 55 miles apart at their closest points across the Bering Strait, while Russia’s Big Diomede Island and Alaska’s Little Diomede Island are separated by roughly 2.5 miles. Alaska also hosts major air bases, early-warning and missile-defense infrastructure and tens of thousands of military personnel. U.S. Northern Command says Alaskan Command has more than 22,000 active-duty personnel from across the services, along with approximately 4,700 Guard and Reserve members. Air Force officials have described Alaska as the "crossroads of the Arctic and the Pacific," providing U.S. forces with reach and domain awareness for both homeland defense and global power projection. Davis put that geography in even starker terms. Pointing to the fifth-generation fighters positioned in Alaska, he told Fox News Digital that U.S. forces can "project from the Arctic to almost anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere in about 10 hours of flight time." RUSSIA’S QUIETER NUCLEAR SUBMARINES THREATEN NATO, FORMER COMMANDER WARNS Tundra Merlin is designed to turn that geographic advantage into combat capability. Davis described the operation as a collection of military options — essentially "plays in a playbook" — that can be activated either to deter an adversary or respond if one begins acting aggressively. "Our hope is that we don’t have any adversarial activity because we’ve effectively deterred it," Davis said. "But if we do see it and we have kind of a play in the playbook ready to go. For a response."One of the most striking demonstrations came in recently, on Alaska’s western edge. U.S. and Canadian forces rapidly moved a U.S. Army HIMARS mobile rocket system and an AN/TPQ-53 radar into western Alaska aboard a Royal Canadian Air Force C-17, then connected those ground forces with American F-35s, F-16s and a KC-135 tanker operating overhead. CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS The mission brought air defense and long-range offensive firepower together in a single operation. F-35s and HIMARS synchronized against a simulated ground target approximately 135 miles away, while F-16s simultaneously intercepted F-35s acting as simulated incoming aerial threats, according to U.S. Northern Command. Davis said the point was not simply to prove the individual weapons worked, but to show how quickly forces could be moved into a remote part of Alaska and linked together. The operation demonstrated that U.S. forces can rapidly move capabilities into Alaska "both to defend Alaska, but also, if necessary, to put other adversary targets at risk," he told Fox News Digital. Tundra Merlin pushed that same concept out to sea in September. From Sept. 18–22, U.S. and Canadian forces conducted a joint maritime strike scenario roughly 100 nautical miles north of Dutch Harbor, integrating U.S. Coast Guard and Royal Canadian Navy surface and subsurface vessels with Canadian maritime patrol aircraft and Alaska-based U.S. Air Force F-35 fighters and E-3 airborne warning and control aircraft. The forces practiced multiple simulated maritime target engagements, testing whether information collected by different ships and aircraft could be rapidly passed across the force and used to identify, track and engage a potential threat. "The most impressive part to me was seeing the high degree of cooperation and integration amongst units that day in and day out don't necessarily operate together," Davis said. "To see the joint nature on the U.S. side integrated together with the inter-agency of the U.S. Coast Guard and with our allies, with Canada as an example, was just an amazing thing to see," he added. That ability to operate at scale is complicated by Alaska itself. Extreme cold can affect equipment and personnel, while the enormous distances and limited infrastructure of the North American Arctic make moving and sustaining forces unusually difficult. The Pentagon’s Arctic Strategy specifically identifies those distances and the region’s infrastructure limitations as obstacles to military operations and says maintaining infrastructure in Alaska is essential for missile defense, surveillance and rapid power projection. Davis said military equipment brought into Alaska cannot simply be expected to function as it would elsewhere. "It needs to be conditioned. It needs to be properly outfitted to operate in sub-zero temperatures for a long period of time," he said, adding that troops also require specialized clothing, training and procedures to avoid cold-weather injuries and continue fighting in Arctic conditions. The pressure to master that environment comes as Russia and China increasingly demonstrate their own ability to operate near North America. In July 2024, the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, detected and intercepted two Russian Tu-95 bombers and two Chinese H-6 bombers flying together in the Alaskan Air Defense Identification Zone . It was the first time NORAD had intercepted Russian and Chinese military aircraft operating together in the zone. The aircraft remained in international airspace and did not enter U.S. or Canadian sovereign territory, and NORAD said the flight itself was not considered a threat. The episode nevertheless highlighted the very kind of cooperation U.S. defense planners are watching. For now, Davis said Alaska is positioned to deal with the military threats commanders expect under normal conditions. "We're postured very well for any of the anticipated threats that we think would come our way in the very near term," he said. But if commanders saw indications of a significant escalation, Davis said Alaskan Command would likely request additional forces and capabilities. articles.title: 'Went out to play': 4 school students found dead in Thiruneermalai lake near Chennai
articles.summary: CHENNAI: Four school students who went missing on October 3 were found dead in Thiruneermalai lake near Chromepet on Sunday, police said.
articles.body: CHENNAI: Four school students who went missing on October 3 were found dead in Thiruneermalai lake near Chromepet on Sunday, police said.The deceased, all residents of Krishna Street in Lakshmipuram, were identified as Pooja, 13, Khushi, 13, K Devadarshan, 12, and Yuvanesh, 10.The two girls were studying in Class VIII, while the boys were in Classes VII and VI, respectively, police told news agency PTI.The children had gone out to play in their neighbourhood on Saturday but did not return home.Their parents and relatives searched for them and circulated their photographs in local WhatsApp groups, but could not trace them.Separate missing-person complaints were subsequently filed at Chromepet police station late Saturday night.Around 10am on Sunday, residents spotted four bodies floating in Thiruneermalai Periya Eri and alerted the authorities.Personnel from the Tamil Nadu Fire and Rescue Services (TNFRS) reached the spot and recovered the bodies, police said.A preliminary investigation suggested that the children may have entered the lake to bathe and drowned after getting trapped in the slush, police said.Family members identified the bodies, which were then sent to the Tambaram District Government Hospital mortuary for postmortem examination.Police have registered a case, and further investigation is underway.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: City govt colleges seek new courses such as data science, AI and defence studies to attract toppers
articles.summary: Chennai city govt colleges seek approval for new UG courses like data science, AI and defence studies to attract toppers as 2026-27 seats near full.
articles.body: Chennai: To attract toppers, govt colleges in the city sought approval from the govt to start trendingcourses such as data science, artificial intelligence, defence studies and business management courses at the undergraduate level.Most of the city colleges have filled more than 90% of their intake for the 2026-27 academic year. However, colleges said courses such as history, economics and maths could not attract students as students are interested in studying emerging technologies even in the arts and science stream.Govt Arts College in Nandanam has filled more than 90% of seats of its 1,430 sanctioned strength for the 2026-27 academic year.“We have attracted more top-ranking students after the college became co-ed last year. We wanted to offer courses such as data science, AI and defence studies to attract top rankers,” a professor who involved in admissions in the college said.The college has submitted a proposal to govt on new courses.As of now, only two govt colleges, including Dr Ambedkar Arts College at Vyasarpadi, are offering a defence studies course which is very popular across the state.“The defence course attracted more than 4,000 applications for 50 seats. Students who want to join the armed forces are interested in defence studies. However, there are no permanent faculty member to offer the programme. The college employed guest faculty through PTA,” a faculty member from the college said.Presidency College, which has attracted more than 45,000 applications against a sanctioned intake of 2,380, also plans to start new courses such as BBA, defence studies and communication courses for the next academic year.“The state govt should start courses such as BA defence studies with new faculty members in more govt colleges. There is a demand for courses such as sociology, public administration and microbiology as well,” said S Suresh, general secretary, Tamil Nadu Govt Collegiate Teachers’ Association (TNGCTA).According to the data from the Directorate of Collegiate Education, 97,244 seats out of 1,26,959 seats were filled in 181 colleges for the 2026-27 academic year.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: Trichy MP vows to push for revision of 2007 road safety policy
articles.summary: Trichy MP Durai Vaiko vows to push Tamil Nadu to revise its 2007 road safety policy, backing district action plans, speed guidelines and 2030 death cuts.
articles.body: Trichy: Stressing the need for a comprehensive State Road Safety Action Plan with actionable district-level plans to reduce road deaths, Citizen consumer and civic Action Group (CAG), Chennai, hosted a stakeholder workshop with Tamil Nadu Consumer Federation in Trichy on Sunday.The workshop discussed the need for Tamil Nadu to update its Road Safety Policy, which the state pioneered in 2007, ahead of the National Road Safety Policy, 2010.“No matter what road safety action plan or policy we bring, roads will become safer only if we obey the rules. Even on my way here, I watched a person violate a red signal, and many followed him. The change for safer roads should come from us, including elected representatives. I will apprise the need for revising the state’s road safety policy with the CM,” Durai Vaiko said.The MP said infrastructure improvements being carried out through his efforts at G Corner, Sanjeevi Nagar and Kollidam Y road junctions in the city would make roads safer.Tamil Nadu recorded 67,526 road crashes in 2024, the highest in the country. Trichy district recorded 720 road crash casualties in 2023, while fatalities stood at 816 in 2024 and 529 in 2025.Researchers from CAG, Chennai, said a structured State Road Safety Action Plan was critical to achieving the national goal of reducing road crash deaths by 50% by 2030.“Speed guidelines must be urgently implemented as speeding is the primary cause of crashes and fatalities on the roads,” Nina Subramani, Senior Researcher, CAG, said.
